Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. New Pour says what's in the glass and the brand's posture at the same time. The brand sits on the act of opening something modern, the bottle that wasn't on the list last year.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern wine retail has been moving toward natural wine, low-intervention producers, and design-led shop fronts. Customers are design-literate, slightly burnt out on long origin stories, and looking for shops that respect their time.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Discovery Wines (discoverywines.com) holds the modern shop position. Henry & Son (henryandson.co) sits in the design-led tier. Verve Wine (vervewine.com) does the editorial-led middle. Wine.com (wine.com) is the mass-market giant. We sit closer to Henry & Son in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern wine shop that picks the bottle so you don't have to read four paragraphs first.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Buys wine weekly. Already follows two natural wine accounts. Wants the shop to filter the noise. Will pay a premium for editorial taste.

dos: Show the producer, the region, the price
Write tasting notes in plain English
donts: Use the word terroir without explaining it
Write tasting notes that say 'forest floor'

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. NEW POUR in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, a single tilted rectangle suggesting a wine glass viewed from the side, used as the favicon and on the shipping carton seal.

colorPalette.name: Pour Red
colorPalette.meaning: The single accent. The color of a young red.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for vintages and prices
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the vintage and the price. The regular carries the brand and the editorial copy.

customSections.body: A site that loads the weekly recommendation first. A small shop with a printed list reprinted weekly. A monthly newsletter with three bottles and what to cook with them. No app.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two names with French rhythm. Petit suggests smallness and care. Côte is the wine term for a slope (Côte d'Or, Côte Rôtie). The pair reads as a small heritage merchant with a quiet cellar of important bottles.
Luxury.story: Petit & Côte was founded by two principals who had spent decades inside larger fine wine houses and wanted to keep a smaller cellar. The firm represents a limited number of producers. Some clients have been buying through the firm since it opened.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end fine wine has been moving toward larger auction houses and faster transactions. There's a parallel market for small merchants with deep relationships, both with producers and with collectors. The customer is paying for the merchant's eye, not the catalog.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Berry Bros. & Rudd (bbr.com) holds the institutional London reference. Acker Merrall & Condit (ackerwines.com) sits in the auction-meets-merchant tier. Skurnik Wines (skurnikwines.com) does the importer-led version in the US. We sit smaller and quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small fine wine merchant with a private list and a long client book.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often inherited. Builds a cellar over decades. Trusts a small number of merchants by name. Values the relationship with the principal.

dos: Name the producer, the vineyard, the vintage

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the firm's hallmark, used on labels, the printed allocation cards, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles the few digital surfaces.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Glass is the unit of wine drinking. The brand sits on the object, not the bottle, not the vintage, not the maker. Plain, honest, and slightly disarming.
Minimal.industrySummary: Wine brands have elaborate names and longer stories. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the smallest object in the experience.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most wine brands fail this purity test. The closest peer in spirit is some Japanese sake brands and the no-name aesthetic of Muji's table wine line, if it existed.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A small wine list of bottles meant to be poured by the glass.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who order wine by the glass and don't want to read a wine list. They want one to three good options at known prices.

dos: Show the wine, the price by the glass

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. GLASS in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, five letters with generous space. No icon. The bar menu, the bottle shop label, and the receipt all carry the wordmark and nothing else.

typography.rationale: One face. The menu, the website, and the receipt all carry the same wordmark.

Corporate.tagline: Wine distribution and import at scale.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Vineyard signals the source. Holdings Group names the corporate structure. The whole name reads like a real, established wine importer and distributor already on the panel at major retailers and restaurant groups.
Corporate.industrySummary: Wine importing and distribution is a serious B2B category dominated by major importers (Southern Glazer's, RNDC, Breakthru) and a few specialist firms. The buyers are retail chains, restaurant groups, and on-premise operators. Brand and operational discipline are the differentiators.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits (southernglazers.com) holds the giant peer position. RNDC (rndc-usa.com) sits at the same tier. Skurnik Wines (skurnikwines.com) does the design-led import middle. We sit smaller, focused on the contemporary fine wine and natural wine middle market.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Wine importing and distribution for fine wine retailers and restaurant groups at scale.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Retailers and restaurant groups want partners who can deliver consistent fine wine and natural wine supply at scale. The category incumbents are designed for legacy distribution. We are designed for the contemporary buyer.

targetAudience.primary: Beverage Directors, Wine Buyers, and Category Managers at retail chains, restaurant groups, and on-premise operators. They sign multi-year contracts.
motivations: Reliable supply across producers and regions
Design-led catalog development without losing operational discipline

dos: Lead with the catalog and the delivery model

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Second Bottle is the moment a dinner gets good. The brand names the threshold of a real conversation. Loud, warm, and slightly cheeky.
Creative.manifesto: Most wine brands sell the first sip. The reverent moment. The notes on the back of the label. We made Second Bottle because the truth about wine is that the second one is when things get interesting. The brand is for the dinner that runs long, the conversation that gets honest, the moment people stop pretending to know what tannin means.
Creative.industrySummary: Wine branding has been earnest, terroir-led, and slightly precious. There's room for a brand that's loud, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and serious about good wine without taking itself too seriously.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Black Lips Brewing isn't wine but does this voice. Big Bad Wines (bigbadwines.com) sits closer. Some Young Punks (someyoungpunks.com) holds the irreverent label position. We sit warmer and more retail-friendly than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A wine brand for the dinner that runs long.

dos: Write tasting notes in real English

donts: Use the word terroir without translating
